report:
Based on the evidence, the "yes" answer needs important nuance—current research is suggestive but not conclusive.

## What the Evidence Shows

**Bone density effects are modest but real.** Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show whole-body vibration (WBV) can modestly reduce bone loss, particularly in the lumbar spine, in postmenopausal women (Springer/BioMed Central meta-analysis: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-016-0357-2). However, effects on femoral neck BMD are less consistent, and gains are generally smaller than those from resistance/impact training programs like the LIFTMOR trial.

**Fracture-specific evidence is limited but encouraging.** A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis in *Bone* found WBV reduced fracture risk in generally healthy older adults without chronic illness, and concluded WBV "may be a safe and beneficial supplementary treatment for osteoporosis and help prevent fractures" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0965229922000139). Importantly, this benefit was clearer in healthy populations than in those with comorbidities.

**Falls-prevention pathway matters most.** A BMJ Open systematic review/meta-analysis (≥50 years) found WBV significantly reduced fall rates, and since falls are the proximate cause of most osteoporotic fractures, this indirect mechanism is a key contributor to fracture reduction (https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342). Direct fracture-incidence data from trials remain sparse, since most studies use BMD as a surrogate endpoint rather than tracking actual fractures.

**Caution warranted for frail/chronic-disease populations.** Reviews on WBV for fracture prevention in people with chronic diseases (e.g., PMC review on senile osteoporosis) note effects are less certain and safety/efficacy need more study in frailer groups (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9925023/).

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a qualified "yes": WBV appears to reduce fracture risk mainly by improving bone density modestly and, more robustly, by reducing falls—but it should be viewed as an adjunct to (not replacement for) standard osteoporosis treatment, with strongest evidence in healthier older adults.
